title: Value Investing Isn't Holding Long — It's Stashing a Big Pile in the Bank First
dek: No value investor ever went from broke to rich doing value investing; they made money first, then chose to live the value-investing life. Buffett's real engine is 60 to 70 wholly owned subsidiaries pumping cash, not a compounding myth.
why: This episode is dense, but the guest's judgments are quite absolute, and the host explicitly registers partial reservations at the end. For anyone who wants a complete, counterintuitive teardown.
who: Investors who already believe in value investing but haven't thought through where the principal and cash flow come from, and founders who want to understand Buffett's actual wealth structure.
skip: The host's closing monologue after about 1:43 is optional; the guest portion before it is denser.

points.h: The story of the two old ladies in heaven is something we made up
points.body: In 1999, new apartments along Beijing's Third and Fourth Ring Roads sold for 4,000 yuan per square meter and wouldn't move; single-story courtyard houses inside the city cost only a few hundred yuan per square meter, and people didn't want to borrow from banks — they felt shame about debt. Fang Yan was working at an ad agency then. To convince the market, he first had to convince the people around him, so in the office he fabricated the story of the Chinese old lady who saved her whole life to buy a house and the American old lady who took out a loan, bought a house, and finished paying it off just before she died — then pushed it out through the media. Once he believed it himself, he bought his first place in 2000, set a rule of one per year, and designed his life to retire at 40. The detail shows: many wealth beliefs treated as common sense trace back to a single marketing campaign.

points.h: Companies that sell advice can't go public
points.body: Fang Yan ran an ad agency early on. His clients went public one after another, so he asked a securities firm whether they could take him public too. The answer: your kind of company is called a ‘people-based company’ — you sell ideas, and to come up with more ideas you have to hire more people. Only a ‘capital-based company’ that pools money together generates enormous force, and only that is suited to going public. Restaurants are the least suited to listing, because one location being delicious doesn't mean a hundred will be; Haidilao could list because it first built a condiment factory and had a standardized product. That classification directly determined his later decision to give up the billionaire dream and buy stocks instead — ‘once you buy a stock, you are the listed company.’

points.h: Munger said value investing is a big pile of money in the bank
points.body: At the Daily Journal shareholder meeting, someone asked what value investing is, and Munger's answer wasn't the textbook line: keep a large sum in the bank, then patiently wait for an opportunity. Fang Yan thinks this is the truth — no value investor ever went from broke to rich doing value investing; they made money first, then chose to live the value-investing life. India's Pabrai also sold his company, put a big pile in the bank, and then waited for opportunities. The companion rule is ‘if you want to be a value investor, you have to live the value-investing life’: Buffett keeps three to four hundred billion US dollars in cash in the bank, and has lived for over fifty years in a $30,000 house in a fourth-tier city.

points.h: Buffett's engine is 60 to 70 subsidiaries, not compounding
points.body: Fang Yan breaks it down: over fifty years of doing business, Buffett gained control of 60 to 70 wholly owned subsidiaries, and those subsidiaries in turn control several hundred grandchild companies. The CEOs' job is to endlessly generate free cash flow, but they have no right to allocate it — the cash flows up to Berkshire, where a few big heads allocate it. The insurance group contributes only about a quarter of revenue; more comes from companies making gloves, old work boots, T-shirts, hats, bricks, wedding rings, DQ ice cream, See's Candies — the eating, drinking, and daily life of ordinary people. These businesses don't need outstanding CEOs; almost anyone can follow the rules. So Buffett isn't 100% trading stocks — he controls a large real-economy conglomerate in America.

points.h: If you've never run a company, you can't understand one
points.body: Duan Yongping said ‘you'd best run a company,’ and Fang Yan says that line stings as much as Munger's: unless you go build a company yourself, hire people, negotiate with clients, and get hurt by clients, you don't know how complex the business world is. His experience as a boss is that ‘there is no company that doesn't lose money’ — embezzlement, employee negligence, fake invoices for reimbursement — it's unavoidable. That's why he won't invest in restaurants. He also cites a brand caught up in a scandal: it claimed 6 billion a year, and on a single-brand basis profit was 300 million, yet at the group level it was losing money — essentially it was selling vegetables for others for free, and the money was earned by the vegetable and soy sauce sellers and by mall landlords.

points.h: The 80/20 rule understates it — it's 2% winning and 98% losing
points.body: Fang Yan believes that over a long horizon it isn't 20% winning and 80% losing, but 2% of people making money and 98% being losers. His own experience: in March 2015 he withdrew his money from the GF Securities branch at SOHO on the East Third Ring Road, and the manager walked him out and said that in their entire branch only two people had made big money. What he withdrew was 120 million yuan, on principal of just over 13 million. Three months later the whole market collapsed and no one could get out. He forced his nephew to get out too; the nephew couldn't resist and went back in, and he had to force him out again.

points.h: Tie yourself to the mast or you won't hold onto the money
points.body: After withdrawing the 120 million, the market kept rising — a single day's gain could be over ten million — and Fang Yan himself was struggling. His method was to go to ICBC and buy a product he couldn't withdraw: a bond issued by ICBC, benchmarked to foreign exchange, contracted in six-month terms, paying 10,000 yuan a day, but absolutely not redeemable. He says there's only one way to tie yourself down, and it's a physical method — the equivalent of Odysseus tying himself to the mast and having his crew plug their ears with wax. The day the market collapsed, June 15, happened to be his wife's birthday; the whole restaurant was sighing and panicking, and only their table was happy and relaxed.

points.h: Buying jets, chasing celebrities, climbing Everest are reverse indicators
points.body: Fang Yan says this isn't a curse, it's objective reality: no one has climbed Everest and then had their business thrive afterward. Climbing Everest is a show-off mentality; getting up isn't that hard, since a Sherpa team helps you, and with two-plus months of back-and-forth training the cost is enormous. Zhang Chaoyang himself reflected on it, saying that for Everest he spent several months away from the company, and that it was the single thing he most shouldn't have done. Being away from the company year-round while employees watch you climb Everest on TV every day changes the team's mindset. Private jets are the same: in the US they're bought by 20 or 30 people crowdfunding, and with vast, sparsely populated land and inconvenient transport there's an objective need; China has no such need, and this game was played once here — fewer and fewer people are buying now.

quotes.text: So we made up that famous story — the two old ladies meeting in heaven — that was made up, that was us.
No value investor ever went from broke to being a value investor and became a tycoon. None. Every value investor made money first, and then chose to live the value-investing life.

If you don't go build a company yourself, don't hire people, don't negotiate with clients, don't get hurt by clients, you don't know how complex the business world is, and you can't understand a company.
There's only one way to tie yourself down — you have to think of a physical way to tie yourself down.
The most terrifying thing is always this: you take three steps forward and one step back — that's hesitation. The most terrifying thing is indecision, and then half-believing, half-doubting.
